intro: This is Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 concert reworking, not Mussorgsky’s original 1867 orchestral score. How does the long quiet ending alter your memory of the witches’ gathering?
question: What changes when the restless music gives way to stillness?

sections.label: Renewed orchestral pressure
sections.mNote: opening agitation and heavy orchestral answers regain their weight

relations.label: The opening agitation returns
relations.basis: In Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert version, opening fast material returns after contrasting episodes; these excerpts link the opening with the renewed-pressure section marked near 365 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.924, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 343.5 s (cache/form/mussorgsky-night-bald-mountain.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Motion before a broad tune
cues.text: The opening combines rapid figures with heavier, separated gestures. Listen to the relationship between the moving surface and the lower accents: different rates of activity can coexist without all the parts doubling one another.
cues.evidence: This describes the opening texture of Rimsky-Korsakov’s version; no individual instrument entrance is inferred from the recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An officer leaves service
cues.text: Mussorgsky received a Guards commission in 1856 and resigned it in 1858. He studied composition with Balakirev outside the conservatory system and began civil-service work in 1863.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research’s Mussorgsky biography records the commission, resignation, lessons and civil-service appointment.

cues.title: Quieter does not mean inactive
cues.text: The lighter passages keep short attacks in motion even as the overall sound recedes. Follow those small figures independently of the larger surges: a quiet stretch need not be a pause in the activity.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls around 1:20 while frequent detected attacks continue through the following half-minute.

cues.title: The upper edge of sound
cues.text: Through this passage, compare the high activity with the heavier lower accents. Changes in register and colour can sharpen a phrase without replacing its underlying rhythmic material.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a marked increase in upper-frequency energy around 2:30–2:45; it does not identify the contributing instruments.

cues.title: Balakirev rejects the score
cues.text: Mussorgsky completed his original orchestral version in 1867. Balakirev rejected it, and it was not performed in the composer’s lifetime; Mussorgsky later reworked the material for stage projects.
cues.evidence: The LA Phil programme note distinguishes the 1867 score, Balakirev’s rejection and the subsequent stage versions.

cues.title: Broader spans between attacks
cues.text: Around this part of the piece, compare the longer-held sound with the opening’s restless figures. A phrase can maintain pressure through sustained notes as well as through repeated attacks.
cues.evidence: The analysis finds less frequent attacks around 4:40–4:50 despite a high relative level; no key change is established by that measurement.

cues.title: Repeated surges, not one crescendo
cues.text: The central stretch alternates strong surges with brief withdrawals. Follow the shape of successive phrases rather than hearing the whole gathering as one uninterrupted increase in force.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 5:35, recedes by 5:45 and reaches another strong peak near 6:05.

cues.title: An editor’s concert piece
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov completed this version in 1886, five years after Mussorgsky’s death. He drew especially on the later choral stage version; the concert piece involves selection and recomposition, not merely a new orchestration of the 1867 score.
cues.evidence: The LA Phil note quotes Rimsky-Korsakov’s account of selecting from the surviving materials and explains the Sorochyntsi Fair connection.

cues.title: Withdrawal before another climb
cues.text: This later stretch contains a marked drop in level followed by renewed force. Listen for how the quieter starting point changes the effect of the next build-up, even before it reaches its peak.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls by about 12 dB around 7:15–7:20, then recovers strongly by 7:40.

cues.title: Before the quiet aftermath
cues.text: The late fast passage gathers force before the long quiet ending. Keep the closely packed figures in memory so that you can compare their pace with the more sustained writing to come.
cues.evidence: A high-level, bright passage around 8:00–8:10 precedes a substantial withdrawal around 8:20.

cues.title: From gathering to daybreak
cues.text: The transition towards daybreak replaces the gathering’s fast activity with a long quiet aftermath. In this version’s scenario, a church bell disperses the gathering; listen for the broader contrast, not a bell stroke at this note’s display time.
cues.evidence: The score and scenario identify the bell; strong changes around 8:20–8:32 support the transition’s approximate location, not the bell’s onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An unfinished comic opera
cues.text: Mussorgsky reused the sabbath material in his unfinished opera The Fair at Sorochyntsi, after Gogol. That stage version became a principal source for Rimsky-Korsakov’s later concert piece.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research documents the unfinished Gogol opera; the LA Phil note identifies its music as a source of the concert reworking.

cues.title: The sustained lower foundation
cues.text: Through the quiet aftermath, attend to the low foundation beneath the longer phrases. The reduction in rapid activity leaves more space to follow how an upper line moves against a sustained bass.
cues.evidence: This is a passage-level listening guide; the analysis finds few attacks and a persistent low D estimate across much of 8:40–10:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Repin at the hospital
cues.text: In 1881 Ilya Repin painted Mussorgsky in the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital in Saint Petersburg. The portrait shows him in a dressing gown; the composer died in the same city that March, shortly after his forty-second birthday.
cues.evidence: Mussorgsky.ru’s portrait record locates the sitting in the hospital; Tchaikovsky Research gives his birth and death dates.

cues.title: A different kind of close
cues.text: The ending sustains a D major destination rather than returning to the opening rush. Compare the space between gestures with the rapid figures at the beginning: the long aftermath is part of this version’s design.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the major-key close; the final analysis windows show little attack activity and support that tonal destination only approximately.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Heavy summons become lighter repeated figures
transitions.how: In Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert version, the opening’s rapid string motion and heavy orchestral proclamations give way to lighter, more detached dance figures. The D-minor frame remains unsettled by chromatic notes, but the change is chiefly in articulation and weight: short wind-and-string gestures keep moving after the larger brass-led attacks recede. The bass still gives the figures a pulse, so a reduction in orchestral mass does not stop the gathering’s activity.
transitions.evidence: The Dance figures boundary is 1:20, a strong novelty peak; relative level falls while detected attacks remain frequent through 1:50. The description follows the contrasting orchestral textures of Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 score, not Mussorgsky’s 1867 original. The report does not separate instruments or establish a new key here.

transitions.title: The opening material regains orchestral weight
transitions.how: The contrasting episodes are drawn back towards the opening’s D-minor agitation. Short, sharply accented figures and the heavier orchestral answer recover the original opposition between restless motion and proclamation. Rimsky-Korsakov makes recognition itself a join: familiar material returns with full weight instead of being introduced by a separate linking tune. The bass and lower orchestral accents again confront the quicker upper activity.
transitions.evidence: The Renewed pressure boundary is 6:05, the report’s strongest five-second relative-level window. The relations file matches 21.5–37 s with 365–380.5 s, provisionally identifying the return of opening material. The score supplies the D-minor framework and contrasting orchestral layers; no detailed pivot-chord route is claimed.

transitions.title: The bell removes the fast music’s foundation
transitions.how: The final fast accumulation is interrupted by the church bell, and the gathering’s figures break apart rather than completing another dance paragraph. Brass weight and rapid orchestral activity withdraw; sustained strings and exposed wind phrases take over. The harmonic destination changes from D minor to D major, retaining the tonic while F♮ gives way to F♯. In this concert version, the bell is a structural intervention: it replaces the fast music’s continuity with a slower, sustained aftermath.
transitions.evidence: The Bell boundary is 8:20, with strong novelty at 8:20 and 8:32; relative level falls from −7.6 dB at 8:10 to about −30 dB at 8:20–8:35. The bell, dispersal and major-key aftermath are features of Rimsky-Korsakov’s score and scenario. The extended span does not claim the bell’s exact onset.

transitions.title: The tonic remains after the figures disperse
transitions.how: The slow conclusion does not prepare a return of the sabbath. Rimsky-Korsakov prolongs D as a low foundation while solo woodwind lines and sustained strings replace the earlier massed gestures. D-major harmony is coloured by passing inflections, but the bass no longer propels a chain of fast episodes. The join is a further reduction of activity within the aftermath: longer phrases and the space between them now carry the music towards its quiet major-key close.
transitions.evidence: The Quiet aftermath boundary is 10:02, a strong novelty peak amid sparse attacks and sustained low relative level. The score supplies the sustained D foundation, exposed wind writing and D-major conclusion. The relations file rejects late harmonic matches as independent formal returns; this transition likewise describes continuation, not a new reprise.

facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
